title: Disability Sport as Institution
bigQuestion: How did disabled athletes build their own games, federations and rule books, and win a place beside the Olympics?

story.title: A Card Beside a Racing Chair
story.kicker: Before a wheelchair race, a small card says which class the racer belongs to.
paragraphs: A racing wheelchair rests near the start of a track. It has three wheels, a long low frame and no armrests. Next to it lies a card from a classification panel. The card names the athlete's sport class. In wheelchair track racing, one class is written T54. The letter T stands for track.

The card works a little like a ticket. It lets the athlete enter races against others whose impairments affect the sport in a similar way. A panel of trained classifiers gave the card. The panel may include a doctor or a physical therapist and an expert in the sport. The athlete can ask for a review if the class seems wrong.

That card is the product of more than a century of institution building. Deaf athletes held their first international games in Paris in 1924. Doctors and veterans started wheelchair games after World War II. Coaches in Illinois founded a national wheelchair basketball association in 1949. The International Paralympic Committee was founded in 1989.

Each step made a new office, a new rule book or a new championship. Disabled athletes and their allies ran many of these bodies themselves. The racing chair and the card together show sport, not charity. Records are kept, results are official and medals are won.
story.think: Why might athletes want a card and a class instead of one open race for everyone?

lessons.title: A College Team in Washington
lessons.mainIdea: Gallaudet, founded in 1864, gave deaf students a college with its own teams and a sports life run in sign language.
reading: In 1864 President Abraham Lincoln signed a law that let a school in Washington, D.C., grant college degrees. The school became *Gallaudet* University, named for Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet. He had helped open the first lasting American school for deaf students, in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1817.

By the late 1800s, many state schools for the deaf had teams. So did Gallaudet. Players and coaches talked in sign language. Deaf schools played hearing schools in their towns, so their teams were part of local sport from early on.

A well known story says the football huddle began at Gallaudet in the 1890s. In it, quarterback Paul Hubbard pulled his team into a circle so other deaf teams could not read their signs. The story is told by the university itself, but written records from the time are thin. Historians treat it as a tradition, not a proven first.

words.d: a university in Washington, D.C., for deaf and hard of hearing students; its college charter dates to 1864
a full language made with the hands, face and body; American Sign Language is used in the United States
a story or practice handed down, which may or may not be proven by records

look.title: Record or Tradition?
look.text: Claim A: In 1864 Abraham Lincoln signed a law letting the school grant college degrees. Claim B: In the 1890s a Gallaudet quarterback invented the football huddle. Claim A is backed by a federal law. Claim B is backed mainly by stories told later.
look.prompt: Which claim would you call a record and which a tradition? What kind of paper would make Claim B stronger?

check.q: Who signed the 1864 law that let Gallaudet grant college degrees?
check.why: President Abraham Lincoln signed the 1864 law.

check.q: Why do historians call the huddle story a tradition?
choices: Written records from the time are thin
check.why: The story is told later, but records from the 1890s do not prove it.

check.q: Where did the first lasting American school for deaf students open in 1817?
check.why: Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet helped open it in Hartford, Connecticut.

lessons.title: The Silent Games of 1924
lessons.mainIdea: In 1924 deaf leaders in Paris held the first international games for deaf athletes and founded a federation to run them.
reading: In August 1924 athletes from several European countries met in Paris for the International Silent Games. The organizer was *Eugène Rubens-Alcais*, a deaf Frenchman who led a French deaf sports federation. The Summer Olympics had been held in Paris a few weeks earlier that same summer.

At the end of the games, leaders founded a governing body. Its French name was the Comité International des Sports des Sourds, or *CISS*. Today it is called the International Committee of Sports for the Deaf. Deaf people have led it from the start, which makes it one of the oldest sport bodies run by disabled people themselves.

The games have been held about every four years since, apart from the World War II years. Winter games were added in 1949. In 2001 the name *Deaflympics* was adopted. To enter, an athlete must have a hearing loss of at least 55 decibels in the better ear, and hearing aids are taken off during competition.

words.d: the deaf French sports leader who organized the 1924 International Silent Games in Paris
the international committee of sports for the deaf, founded in 1924
the name, since 2001, for the international games for deaf athletes first held in 1924
an organization that sets the rules and runs the championships of a sport

look.title: Founding Years of Disability Sport Bodies
look.cite: ICSD, NWBA, Special Olympics and IPC official histories
look.prompt: How many years passed between the deaf committee and the Paralympic committee? What does the gap tell you about who organized first?

check.q: Who organized the 1924 International Silent Games?
check.why: The deaf French leader Eugène Rubens-Alcais organized them in Paris.

check.q: When was the name Deaflympics adopted?
check.why: The games took the name Deaflympics in 2001.

check.q: What makes CISS stand out among early disability sport bodies?
choices: Deaf people led it from the start
It was run by the Olympics
It was founded in the United States
check.why: Deaf leaders founded and ran the committee from 1924.

lessons.title: Dummy Hoy and the Umpire Story
lessons.mainIdea: William Hoy, a deaf outfielder, played major league baseball from 1888 to 1902; the claim that he caused umpire hand signals is a legend.
reading: William *Hoy* lost his hearing as a young child in Ohio. He attended the Ohio School for the Deaf. He played in the major leagues from 1888 to 1902 for several teams. In 1901 he played for the Chicago White Stockings of the new American League, the team that became the White Sox.

In his time, newspapers called him Dummy Hoy. The word was a common, hurtful label for deaf people then. Many writers today use his given name, William, or his nickname Hoy. He was known as a fast runner and a steady outfielder. He communicated with teammates through signs.

A famous story says umpires began using hand signals for balls and strikes because of Hoy. Historians of baseball find no clear record to prove it, and umpire signals may have spread from several sources. The story is best labeled a *legend*. The record that is certain is his long career in the majors.

words.d: William Hoy (1862–1961), a deaf outfielder in the major leagues from 1888 to 1902
a popular story about the past that records do not prove

look.title: Two Sentences About Hoy
look.text: Sentence 1: William Hoy played in the major leagues from 1888 to 1902. Sentence 2: William Hoy is the reason umpires use hand signals. The first can be checked in box scores and team records. The second is repeated often but has no clear proof.
look.prompt: Why might a legend spread faster than a record? Which sentence would you put in a report, and why?

check.q: Which Chicago team did Hoy play for in 1901?
choices: The White Stockings, later the White Sox
check.why: In 1901 Hoy played for the American League's Chicago White Stockings.

check.q: How should the story that Hoy caused umpire signals be labeled?
check.why: Historians find no clear record, so it is a legend.

check.q: Which fact about Hoy is certain?
choices: He played in the majors from 1888 to 1902
check.why: Box scores and team records show his career from 1888 to 1902.

lessons.title: Stoke Mandeville, 1948
lessons.mainIdea: Ludwig Guttmann used sport in a British spinal injury hospital and held the first Stoke Mandeville Games on the day the 1948 London Olympics opened.
reading: *Ludwig Guttmann* was a Jewish neurologist, a doctor of the brain and nerves, in Germany. He fled Nazi Germany in 1939 and settled in Britain. In 1944 he opened a spinal injuries center at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, northwest of London. Many patients were soldiers with injuries to the spinal cord.

At the time, many people with spinal cord injuries died within a few years. Guttmann changed care with turning, skin care and early activity. He used sport as part of rehabilitation, which means rebuilding strength and skills after an injury. Patients played wheelchair polo, archery and basketball.

On July 29, 1948, the London Olympics opened. The same day, Guttmann held the first *Stoke Mandeville Games*, an archery contest for 16 wheelchair athletes, 14 men and 2 women. In 1952 a team of Dutch veterans came, and the event became international. Guttmann hoped such games would one day stand beside the Olympics.

words.d: a German-born Jewish neurologist who led the spinal injuries center at Stoke Mandeville and started its games in 1948
rebuilding strength and skills after an injury or illness
wheelchair games begun at a British hospital in 1948; they grew into the Paralympics

look.title: One Day, Two Openings
look.text: July 29, 1948: in London, thousands watch the Olympic opening at Wembley Stadium. About 40 miles away, 16 patients in wheelchairs compete in archery on a hospital lawn. Few newspapers cover the second event.
look.prompt: Why do you think Guttmann chose the same day as the Olympic opening? What did he want people to compare?

check.q: Why did Guttmann use sport at Stoke Mandeville?
check.why: He used sport to help patients rebuild strength and skills.

check.q: What happened on July 29, 1948?
choices: The first Paralympic Games in Rome
check.why: Guttmann held the first Stoke Mandeville Games as the London Olympics opened.

check.q: What made the games international in 1952?
choices: A Dutch team of veterans took part
check.why: Dutch veterans came in 1952, making the event international.

lessons.title: Veterans and a Tournament in Galesburg
lessons.mainIdea: American veterans played wheelchair basketball after 1945, and in 1949 teams founded the National Wheelchair Basketball Association in Galesburg, Illinois.
reading: After World War II, thousands of American veterans came home with spinal cord injuries. In veterans' hospitals, some began playing basketball from wheelchairs around 1946. Teams formed in California, New England and the Midwest. One California team, the Flying Wheels, toured the country and drew crowds.

*Timothy Nugent* directed a new program for students with disabilities at the University of Illinois. It started in 1948 at a branch campus in Galesburg. In April 1949 Nugent hosted the first National Wheelchair Basketball Tournament there. Teams from several states took part.

At that tournament, the teams founded the *National Wheelchair Basketball Association*, or NWBA. It wrote rules, kept standings and held a national championship every year. It was a governing body like any other sport league. It made wheelchair basketball one of the oldest organized disability team sports in the United States.

words.d: the University of Illinois leader who hosted the first national wheelchair basketball tournament in 1949
the governing body for wheelchair basketball founded in Galesburg, Illinois, in 1949
a person who has served in the armed forces

look.title: What Makes a League?
look.text: Before 1949: hospital teams play each other when they can, and each game follows local habits. After 1949: one association writes shared rules, keeps standings and names a national champion each year.
look.prompt: List two things the NWBA added that turned scattered games into an institution.

check.q: Where was the first National Wheelchair Basketball Tournament held?
check.why: Tim Nugent hosted it in Galesburg, Illinois, in April 1949.

check.q: Who played much of the first wheelchair basketball in America?
check.why: Veterans with spinal cord injuries played in hospitals after the war.

check.q: What did the NWBA do?
choices: Wrote rules, kept standings and held a national championship
check.why: The NWBA was a governing body with rules, standings and a championship.

lessons.title: A Campus Built for Access
lessons.mainIdea: Nugent's program at the University of Illinois grew into an early model of an accessible campus with its own wheelchair sports teams.
reading: In 1949 Nugent's program moved from Galesburg to the main University of Illinois campus in Urbana-Champaign. Students who used wheelchairs lived, studied and played sports there. Nugent pushed the university to add ramps and curb cuts, the sloped cuts in a curb that let a wheelchair roll from sidewalk to street.

The program's teams became famous. The Gizz Kids played wheelchair basketball and later other wheelchair sports. The university also ran buses that could carry wheelchair users around campus. Students with disabilities formed their own groups and helped run the programs.

The Illinois program showed that *access* is a matter of buildings and rules, not only of individual bodies. A student cannot play in a gym he cannot enter. Later national laws on access, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, required the kinds of changes Illinois had tried decades before.

words.d: being able to reach, enter and use a place or program
a sloped cut in a curb that lets a wheelchair move between sidewalk and street
the University of Illinois wheelchair sports teams from Nugent's program

look.title: A Gym Door
look.text: Picture a school gym in 1950. The only door has five steps up from the sidewalk. Inside, there is a basketball court and a locker room down a flight of stairs. Now picture the same gym after a ramp and a wide doorway are added.
look.prompt: Who could use the gym before the change, and who could use it after? Why is this a question about the building, not the athlete?

check.q: Where did Nugent's program move in 1949?
check.why: It moved from Galesburg to the main campus in Urbana-Champaign.

check.q: What is a curb cut?
choices: A sloped cut in a curb for wheelchairs
check.why: A curb cut lets a wheelchair move between sidewalk and street.

check.q: What does the Illinois program show about access?
choices: It depends only on the athlete
It depends on buildings and rules
It was required by law in 1949
check.why: Ramps, curb cuts and buses opened the campus, showing access is about buildings and rules.

lessons.title: Rome, 1960
lessons.mainIdea: The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960, in the same city as the Olympics that year.
reading: In September 1960, the Summer Olympics were held in Rome. Right after them, Guttmann's international wheelchair games were held in Rome too. About 400 athletes from 23 countries took part. Today the International Paralympic Committee counts Rome 1960 as the first *Paralympic Games*.

All athletes in Rome used wheelchairs. Events included archery, swimming, fencing, table tennis and wheelchair basketball. Athletes with other impairments, such as blind athletes and amputees, were added to the games in 1976. The first Winter Paralympics were held in Örnsköldsvik, Sweden, in 1976.

The word Paralympic was first used for the wheelchair games. Later it was explained as meaning beside, or parallel to, the Olympics. That meaning fits Guttmann's hope from 1948. Tokyo hosted both the Olympics and the Paralympics in 1964, and many later hosts did the same.

words.d: the top international games for athletes with physical and visual impairments and some intellectual impairments, first held in Rome in 1960
side by side and at the same level
a difference in how part of the body or mind works

look.title: Countries at the Summer Paralympics
look.prompt: About how many times more countries came to London in 2012 than to Rome in 1960?

check.q: Where were the first Paralympic Games held?
check.why: The IPC counts the 1960 games in Rome as the first Paralympics.

check.q: Which athletes competed at Rome in 1960?
check.why: All athletes in Rome 1960 used wheelchairs; other groups joined in 1976.

check.q: What is the later meaning given to the word Paralympic?
choices: Beside, or parallel to, the Olympics
check.why: The name came to mean parallel to the Olympics.

lessons.title: One Committee, One Host City
lessons.mainIdea: The International Paralympic Committee, founded in 1989, now governs the Paralympics, and since the 2000s one city hosts both Games.
reading: By the 1980s, several groups ran disability sport. There were separate bodies for wheelchair athletes, blind athletes, amputees and athletes with cerebral palsy. Each had its own rules. In 1988 Seoul held the Paralympics in the same venues it had used for the Olympics.

On September 22, 1989, the *International Paralympic Committee*, or IPC, was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany. It became the single governing body for the Paralympic Games. Its headquarters is in Bonn. It works with national Paralympic committees in each country.

In 2001 the IPC and the International Olympic Committee signed an *agreement*. It said a city chosen for the Olympics would also host the Paralympics. Beijing in 2008 was the first host picked under that rule. In the United States, the Olympic committee added Paralympic to its name in 2019.

words.d: the body founded in 1989 that governs the Paralympic Games
a written deal between two organizations about what each will do
a country's body that sends its team to the Paralympics

look.title: The 2001 IOC–IPC Agreement
look.text: The two committees agreed that the city chosen to host the Olympic Games would also host the Paralympic Games, using the same venues and organizing committee.
look.cite: International Olympic Committee and International Paralympic Committee, cooperation agreement, 2001
look.prompt: What did the Paralympics gain from sharing venues and an organizing committee with the Olympics?

check.q: When and where was the IPC founded?
check.why: The IPC was founded on September 22, 1989, in Düsseldorf.

check.q: What did the 2001 agreement say?
choices: The Olympic host city would also host the Paralympics
Deaf athletes must join the IPC
Only wheelchair events would be held
check.why: The IOC and IPC agreed that one city would host both Games.

check.q: Which Games were the first host picked under the one-city rule?
check.why: Beijing 2008 was the first host chosen under the 2001 agreement.

lessons.title: Classes on a Card
lessons.mainIdea: Classification groups athletes by how their impairment affects a sport, and its rules have changed from medical labels to sport-based tests.
reading: Early wheelchair games grouped athletes by the level of their spinal cord injury. Doctors did the sorting. That worked for one kind of injury. It did not work well once blind athletes, amputees and athletes with cerebral palsy joined.

Over the 1980s and 1990s, many sports moved to *functional classification*. That means grouping athletes by what their bodies can do in that sport, not only by a diagnosis. A swimmer and a sprinter with the same impairment may be placed in different classes in their sports.

In 2007 the IPC adopted an Athlete Classification Code, and it has been revised since. The code says who can be a classifier, how athletes are tested and how they can appeal. Each *sport class* has a short label, like T54 in wheelchair track racing. Arguments about fairness in classes are still part of the Paralympic movement.

words.d: the system that groups para athletes so they compete against others with similar abilities in a sport
grouping athletes by what they can do in a sport, not only by a medical diagnosis
the labeled group an athlete competes in, such as T54 in wheelchair track racing
a formal request to have a decision checked again

look.title: Two Ways to Sort
look.text: Way 1, the early system: a doctor reads a medical chart and assigns a group by diagnosis. Way 2, the later system: a panel watches the athlete in the sport and asks how the impairment affects that sport.
look.prompt: Name one reason athletes might prefer Way 2. Name one new argument Way 2 could start.

check.q: What does functional classification look at?
choices: What the athlete can do in that sport
check.why: It groups athletes by how the impairment affects the sport.

check.q: When did the IPC adopt an Athlete Classification Code?
check.why: The IPC adopted the code in 2007 and has revised it since.

check.q: Why did sorting only by spinal injury level stop working well?
check.why: Blind athletes, amputees and athletes with cerebral palsy needed other ways to be grouped.

lessons.title: Special Olympics at Soldier Field
lessons.mainIdea: The first International Special Olympics Summer Games, for athletes with intellectual disabilities, were held at Soldier Field in Chicago in July 1968.
reading: In 1962 Eunice Kennedy Shriver held a summer day camp at her home in Maryland. It was for children and adults with *intellectual disabilities*, which means differences in learning and thinking skills. It showed that campers could take part in sports and games when given the chance.

In Chicago, a Park District teacher named Anne McGlone Burke planned a citywide track meet for athletes with intellectual disabilities. The Chicago Park District worked with the Kennedy Foundation. On July 20, 1968, the first International *Special Olympics* Summer Games opened at Soldier Field. About 1,000 athletes from the United States and Canada came.

Special Olympics grew into a worldwide organization. It uses divisioning, which groups athletes by ability, age and sex so that contests are close. It also holds year-round training, not only one event. Anne Burke later became a justice of the Illinois Supreme Court.

words.d: a difference in learning and thinking skills that begins in childhood
a worldwide sports organization for people with intellectual disabilities, first held as games at Soldier Field in 1968
grouping Special Olympics athletes by ability, age and sex so contests are close

look.title: A Park District Idea
look.text: A city park district runs gyms, pools and fields in every neighborhood. One of its teachers asks: why is there no citywide meet for the athletes in our special recreation programs? The district and a national foundation answer by renting the city's biggest stadium.
look.prompt: Why did it matter that the first games grew out of a public park district, and not only a private charity?

check.q: Where were the first International Special Olympics Summer Games held?
check.why: They opened at Soldier Field in Chicago on July 20, 1968.

check.q: Who planned the Chicago meet that grew into the 1968 games?
check.why: Anne McGlone Burke, a Chicago Park District teacher, planned it.

check.q: What is divisioning in Special Olympics?
choices: Grouping athletes by ability, age and sex
check.why: Divisioning groups athletes so that each contest is close.

lessons.title: Laws That Opened the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Federal laws from 1973 to 1990, and a 2013 letter from the Education Department, required schools to give students with disabilities a fair chance at sports.
reading: In 1973 Congress passed the Rehabilitation Act. Its *Section 504* says programs that receive federal money may not shut people out because of disability. Public schools receive federal money, so the rule covers school sports too. In 1975 a federal law guaranteed a free public education for children with disabilities.

In 1990 the *Americans with Disabilities Act*, or ADA, reached further. It covered public places and many private businesses, including stadiums and gyms. New buildings had to be accessible. Arenas had to offer wheelchair seating spread through the building.

In January 2013 the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights sent a letter to schools. It said students with disabilities must get an equal chance to try out for teams. Schools should make reasonable changes when they do not change the nature of the sport. Where needed, schools should consider separate or allied teams.

words.d: the part of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 that bans disability exclusion in programs receiving federal money
the 1990 federal law requiring access in public places, jobs and many businesses
a fair adjustment that lets a person take part without changing the basic nature of the activity

look.title: The 2013 Letter to Schools
look.text: The Office for Civil Rights told schools that students with disabilities must have an equal opportunity to take part in after-school athletics. Schools may not rely on general ideas about disability, and must judge each student as an individual.
look.cite: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, Dear Colleague Letter on students with disabilities in extracurricular athletics, January 25, 2013
look.prompt: Why would a law tell schools to judge each student as an individual instead of by a general idea?

check.q: Which law says programs with federal money may not shut people out because of disability?
check.why: Section 504, passed in 1973, covers programs that receive federal money.

check.q: What did the ADA of 1990 add?
choices: It covered public places and many private businesses
check.why: The ADA reached public places, jobs and many private businesses such as arenas.

check.q: What did the 2013 letter tell schools?
choices: To give students with disabilities an equal chance to try out
check.why: The Office for Civil Rights said students with disabilities must get an equal chance.

lessons.title: Athletes, Not Poster Children
lessons.mainIdea: Disability rights activists pushed back on charity images and asked that disabled athletes be seen as competitors with records and rights.
reading: For much of the 1900s, many charities raised money with a *poster child*. The poster showed a disabled child and asked the public for pity and gifts. Television telethons did the same, often for many hours. The money helped research and care, but the pictures showed disabled people as people to feel sorry for.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the disability rights movement pushed back. Activists held protests and sit-ins for laws like Section 504. They used the slogan Nothing About Us Without Us. It means disabled people should help make the decisions that affect them.

Disability sport bodies share that idea. Athletes sit on athlete councils in the IPC and in national committees. Results are kept as official *records*, like any other sport. United States law brought Paralympic athletes into the national Olympic committee's work in 1998, through the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

words.d: a child shown on a charity poster to ask the public for money
the organized effort by disabled people to win equal rights and access
an official result, such as a best time, kept by a governing body

look.title: Two Pictures
look.text: Picture 1: a charity poster from the 1950s shows a child in leg braces. The words ask viewers to give so that the child can be helped. Picture 2: a results sheet from a Paralympic final lists each athlete's name, country, sport class and time to the hundredth of a second.
look.prompt: What does each picture say about who the disabled person is? Which one is an institution's record?

check.q: What does the slogan Nothing About Us Without Us mean?
choices: Disabled people should help make decisions that affect them
Games should be held without crowds
check.why: The disability rights slogan asks that disabled people take part in decisions about them.

check.q: Which 1998 law brought Paralympic athletes into the U.S. Olympic committee's work?
choices: The Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act
check.why: The 1998 Ted Stevens act added Paralympic athletes to the committee's work.

check.q: Why did activists object to poster-child images?
choices: They cost too much to print
They showed disabled people mainly as objects of pity
They were banned by the IPC
check.why: The images asked for pity rather than showing people with rights.

review.why: The Deaflympics have their own governing body, founded by deaf leaders in 1924.

choices: The labeled group an athlete competes in
